textbookText: 3. Describe an activity to prove the Pascal's law with diagram.
Ans:- Activity to prove the Pascal’s law
To show that pressure applied at one point in an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions.
Materials Needed: A plastic bottle with a tight lid, Water, A syringe (without needle), Thin rubber
balloon or plastic sheet, Rubber band, Pin to make small holes
Procedure:
1. Take an empty plastic bottle and make 3–4 small holes around it at the same height.
2. Cover the bottle with a balloon or plastic sheet at the top and tighten it using the rubber band.
3. Fill the bottle completely with water and close the top opening tightly.
4. Now press the balloon or push the syringe connected to the bottle.
5. Observe that water comes out of all holes with equal force.
Observation:
When pressure is applied on the water surface, water jets out equally from all holes, meaning the
applied pressure is transmitted equally in all directions.
Conclusion (Pascal’s Law):
Pressure applied on an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions throughout the fluid.
4. Describe an activity to prove Archimedes's principle with diagram
Ans:- An activity to prove Archimedes's principle are,
To show that the loss of weight of a body in water is equal to the weight of water displaced.
Procedure
1. Measure weight in air: Hang the block on the spring balance (as in the diagram). Note the
reading 𝑊𝑎𝑖𝑟. 2. Submerge in water: Lower the block completely into the water without touching the sides or
bottom. Note the new reading 𝑊𝑤𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑟. 3. Calculate buoyant force: 𝐹𝑏 = 𝑊𝑎𝑖𝑟 - 𝑊𝑊𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑟
4. Measure displaced water (optional): Collect displaced water in a measuring cylinder and find
its weight.
Observation:
The loss of weight of the block in water equals the weight of the displaced water.
Conclusion:
This proves Archimedes’s principle:
A body immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
